latin: Qui profunde et intellectualiter diuisionem unitatis uenereae in trinitatem gratiarum, et unitatis fatalis in trinitatem parcarum, et unitatis Saturniae in trinitatem Iouis, Neptunni, et Plutonis, intellexerit, uidebit modum debite procedendi in orphica theologia.
translation: Whoever understands profoundly and intellectually the division of the unity of Venus into the trinity of the Graces, and of the unity of Fate into the trinity of the Fates, and of the Saturnian unity into the trinity of Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto, will see the way of proceeding correctly in Orphic theology.
translation_note: Farmer's edition marks this thesis as the 805th in his cumulative numbering of the whole collection (farmer1998:25827).
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch17, from Latin at farmer1998:25773
doctrine: Farmer's note glosses the 'method of duly proceeding in Orphic theology' as an operation of splitting monadic unities into triads, but the note excerpted breaks off before completing the explanation (farmer1998:25803).
historiography: Busi and Ebgi quote the thesis's Latin in full from their edition, Conclusiones, page 508, n. 10>8 (busi2014:24950), and their index records the thesis discussed at several further points in connection with the Fates and Saturn (busi2014:3941; busi2014:19045).
not_established: Farmer's completed explanation of the 'method of duly proceeding in Orphic theology', beyond the truncated note consulted, is not established by the sources consulted.

A single Farmer cross-reference recorded for this thesis in research-packets/own_10_008.md points to thesis 1.3 (Albert the Great, 'Haec est in quarto modo dicendi per se: homo est homo'), which shows no apparent thematic connection to Orphic theology; it is treated as an artifact of the extraction and not listed under connections.
